newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers occupy smaller roads, highways free.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers occupy smaller roads, highways free.

text.p: Greek farmers used 2,000 tractors to block roads in central Greece on Tuesday but riot police kept main highways kept open.
Convoys of hundreds of tractors were turned back by police in the central region of Thessally although a few farmers managed to occupy briefly two points on the main north-south highway.
There were no clashes, witnesses said.
"We continue our struggle. The first day went well despite the strong police presence which aimed to terrorise the farmers," farmers' representative Thanasis Nasikas told reporters.

The farmers' main roadblock, with more than 1,500 tractors, was outside Drougos village south of Larissa where they occupied an old north-south road. Police said no cars were stranded and that the effect on traffic was minimal.
"Truckers and most motorists don't drive on the old national road. As long as highways are kept open we don't have any problems," a police official said.
Several convoys of hundreds of tractors played hide-and-seek with police throughout the day, luring them away from highway access points to get bogged down in muddy field.
The government waited out a 25-day farmers' road blockade which virtually cut the country in two in December. It has now vowed to keep roads free.
"We have every legal right to preserve normality. We want to prevent a road blockade," government spokesman Dimitris Reppas told reporters.
The government threatened to use force if necessary. The farmers vowed to continue with their plans but said they would not fight with police.
About 5,000 police, many in riot gear, and helicopters were dispatched to the area to prevent the farmers from taking over the roads for a second time.
"Terrorism does not work on farmers. Their problems are so deep that all the helicopters and police will not hinder them," Vangelis Boutas, another farmers' representative, told reporters.

The farmers gave up the December blockade because of the Christmas holidays but vowed to bring their tractors back to highways if their demands for higher price supports, cheaper fuel and tax cuts were not met.
Prime Minister Costas Simitis has turned down most of their demands, saying the state budget could not afford an extra drachma for any specific group.
He said his strict 1997 budget, described as the toughest in 15 years, tight new pay and tax policies, were necessary to turn the ailing economy around.
